newsitem.title: JAPAN: N.Korea reports defence minister dead in new shock.
newsitem.headline: N.Korea reports defence minister dead in new shock.

text.p: North Korea announced on Saturday the death of its defence minister, the third top official to disappear from its leadership ranks in 10 days.
A brief announcement by the communist nation's official Korea Central Radio said Choe Kwang, 78, a former army officer and Minister of the People's Armed Forces, died of a heart attack on Friday.

Choe's death was announced the day after North Korean premier Kang Song-san was replaced apparently for health reasons and 10 days after the country's ideology chief Hwang Jang-yop defected to the South Korean consulate in Beijing.
The changes removed the sixth (Kang), seventh (Choe) and 24th (Hwang) ranked officials from the Stalinist nation's power structure.
Their departure heightened speculation about major turmoil in North Korea's leadership as it struggles to cope with a major famine set off by two years of record floods.

But in what appeared to be an attempt to prove that the country's de facto leader Kim Jong-il was still firmly in control, North Korea mixed in with the news of Kang's replacement and Choe's death an announcement that it will attend a briefing with the United States and South Korea on Korean peace talks.
In a brief statement by the Foreign Ministry, Pyongyang said it would attend a U.S.-South Korean briefing in New York on March 5 to discuss four-way peace talks also involving China.

The four-way talks were proposed last April by Washington and Seoul to defuse tensions -- and eventually bring about a permanent peace -- on the Korean peninsula. The two Koreas remain technically at war since the 1950-53 conflict ended in a truce and not a peace pact.
The news of Choe's death came as U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright arrived in Seoul for talks with South Korean officials expected to focus on Korean peninsula peace efforts.
Choe headed a 1.1 million-strong armed force, backed by several million reservists, that is one of the most feared in Asia.
Choe, a close comrade of North Korea's dead founder Kim Il-sung, was regarded as a key figure in maintaining the elder Kim's son Kim Jong-il in power.
On Friday, Pyongyang Radio announced that Deputy Prime Minister Hong Song-nam had been appointed acting premier to replace Kang, also a close comrade of the elder Kim.

The report, monitored by the Tokyo-based news agency Radiopress, which follows North Korea's media, gave no reason why Hong, 73, was taking over the post of premier. Kang, 66, had been premier since December 1992.
Radiopress analyst Noriyuki Suzuki said Kang had not been seen in public since January 1996 and speculated that the health of the long-time diabetic had deteriorated.
Suzuki said Hong, expected to be confirmed as permanent premier once North Korea's parliament convenes after a three-year recess, has close ties with the Chinese leadership.
Kang, like Hwang, supported an opening of the Stalinist nation to economic reforms to save it from collapse. Two years of devastating floods have set off widespread famine.

Kang was among seven senior North Korean officials thought to be politically close to Hwang and therefore likely targets of an impending purge by a hard-line group headed by Kim Jong-il, said Modern Korea Institute Director Katsumi Sato.
"If Kim's group fails to purge the reformers, it will give the impression that they lack the power to do so, and that would trigger a stampede to the reformist camp," he said.
